title: Null-forgiving operator and ArgumentNullException (runtime guards vs !)
hook: The postfix `!` does nothing at run time — it only hushes the compiler. `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` actually throws and teaches the analyzer the value is safe afterward.

blocks.text: C# gives you two very different tools that look similar in conversation. **Null-conditional operators** (`?.`, `??`, `is not null`) change control flow at run time. The **null-forgiving operator** (`x!`) does not change behavior — Microsoft’s language reference states it evaluates as `x` and only suppresses nullable warnings. **ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull** is a runtime guard that throws immediately and updates null-state analysis via `[NotNull]` attributes.

entries.plainDefinition: Postfix operator that tells the compiler to treat an expression as not-null. Zero run-time effect.
entries.example: `cache.Get(key)!` — still throws if Get returns null.

entries.plainDefinition: If the receiver is null, the whole expression short-circuits to null instead of throwing.
entries.example: `user?.Email?.Length` returns null when any part is null.

entries.plainDefinition: BCL helper that throws ArgumentNullException when the argument is null. Uses CallerArgumentExpression for the parameter name.
Analysis attribute marking that after a method returns, the annotated parameter is not-null.
entries.example: How ThrowIfNull teaches the compiler that `message` is safe after the call.

blocks.text: At public API edges — SQS message handlers, auth middleware, config binding — you need *real* checks, not compiler lies. Interviews listen for whether you reach for `!` or `ThrowIfNull`. A codebase where every Redis lookup ends with `!` is a map of 2 a.m. production pages.

blocks.title: Reach-for order
blocks.body: 1) `?.` and `??` for optional paths. 2) `is not null` when you need a branch. 3) `ThrowIfNull` / `ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace` at public boundaries. 4) `!` only in tests or when you cannot add an attribute the analyzer understands.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Receive possibly-null input
items.body: Deserialized DTOs, SQS bodies, JWT claims, and Redis values may be null even when your annotations say otherwise.

items.title: Throw early with ThrowIfNull
items.body: Fail fast with a clear ArgumentNullException. The `[NotNull]` post-condition updates null-state for the rest of the method.

items.title: Use optional operators for maybe-null paths
items.body: Optional message attributes stay `string?`. Use `?.` and `??` instead of forcing them through `!`.

items.title: Reserve ! for provable analyzer gaps
items.body: Unit tests passing null into non-nullable parameters, or DI/source-generator outputs the analyzer cannot follow.

diagram.title: ! vs ThrowIfNull at run time
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  IN[Input value x] --> Q{x is null?}
  Q -->|yes, used x!| NRE[NullReferenceException later]
  Q -->|yes, ThrowIfNull| ANE[ArgumentNullException now]
  Q -->|no| OK[Safe to use x]
  BANG[x! path] --> WARN[Warning suppressed only]
  THROW[ThrowIfNull path] --> OK

snippet.label: Guard an SQS record — no bang required
snippet.explanation: Lines 3–4: runtime guards plus null-state update. Line 6: `body` is not-null after throws. Lines 7–9: optional attribute stays `string?`; `??` supplies fallback.

snippet.label: Everyday null-conditional operators
snippet.explanation: Lines 2–4: `?.` short-circuits when `msg` or attributes are null. Line 6: `??` provides a default when the chain returns null.

snippet.label: When ! is legitimate
snippet.explanation: Line 2: `null!` passes null into a non-nullable parameter in tests. Lines 5–9: `[NotNullWhen(true)]` lets callers use `trimmed` without `!` after a true return.

blocks.title: Using ! to silence CS8602
blocks.body: If the compiler warns, either the annotation is wrong or you need a real check. `!` hides the mismatch; it does not fix the bug.

blocks.title: Catching NullReferenceException at boundaries
blocks.body: Prefer ArgumentNullException at public entry points. NRE means something slipped past your design; ArgumentNullException names the contract that was violated.

interviewTakeaways: `x!` is warning suppression with identity semantics at run time.
`ThrowIfNull` is a real throw plus a `[NotNull]` post-condition the compiler understands.
`?.` and `??` and `is not null` are everyday tools; `!` is the exception.
commonPitfalls: Using `!` to satisfy CS8602 instead of fixing the annotation or adding a check.
Catching NullReferenceException instead of throwing ArgumentNullException at the boundary.
Forgetting that message.Body can be empty even when the Message object is non-null.

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript `value!` is the same idea: compile-time only. JavaScript still throws if you read `.length` of null.
`?.` and `??` exist in JavaScript and C# with similar short-circuit rules. C# also ships `ThrowIfNull` as a standard library guard.
